text: After a convolution, the feature map is about as large as the image itself, and it records exactly where each pattern occurred, down to the pixel. For recognising objects that precision is more than we need: it matters that there is an edge somewhere around here, not on which exact pixel it starts. Pooling is the step that trades some of that precision for a more compact summary.

The most common form is max pooling. We split the feature map into small windows, usually two by two, and keep only the largest value in each, which is like summarising each neighbourhood by its strongest signal. With a stride of two the windows do not overlap, so the width and the height are both halved and only a quarter of the numbers remain. Average pooling keeps the mean of each window instead, and it is often used at the very end of a network.

Pooling also buys a little robustness. If a feature shifts by a single pixel but stays inside the same window, the maximum does not change, so the output stays the same. Small shifts and wobbles in the input therefore matter less to the layers that follow, which is what we want when the same object can appear slightly to the left or to the right.

The more important effect is on what each later neuron can see. A neuron in the first convolution looks at a three by three patch of pixels. After pooling, each value summarises a larger region, so a three by three kernel in the next layer covers a much wider patch of the original image. This window on the input, called the receptive field, grows with every layer, until neurons near the top can respond to most of the image.

That growing view is what lets features form a hierarchy. When researchers visualised what trained networks respond to, they found that the first layers detect edges and blobs of colour, middle layers respond to textures and simple shapes, and deeper layers to parts and whole objects, such as wheels or the faces of dogs. Each layer combines the patterns of the layer below into something larger and more meaningful.

Pooling is not sacred. Many modern networks replace it with convolutions of stride two, which shrink the map while letting the network learn how to summarise, and most end with a global average that collapses each channel to a single number. Language models have no pooling between layers, but a similar layering appears: probing studies suggest that earlier layers capture more about individual words and syntax, while later ones capture more abstract meaning.

So pooling shrinks feature maps while widening what each later neuron sees, which lets simple features grow into complex ones. Next we assemble everything into a complete convolutional network, from pixels to a prediction.
